title: Hoelun Raises Her Sons Alone on the Steppe
text:
The Secret History of the Mongols, written in the thirteenth century, tells the early life of Temujin, later Genghis Khan. His mother, Hoelun, had been carried off by his father, Yesugei, from her Merkit bridegroom. When Temujin was about nine, Yesugei was poisoned by Tatars on his way home.

The clan that had followed Yesugei, the Tayichiud, saw no future in a widow with young children. One spring they broke camp and left the family behind. Hoelun seized the clan standard, mounted her horse, and rode after them, shaming some into turning back, but they did not stay. She was left with her sons and the family of Yesugei's second wife, with almost nothing.

The Secret History describes how she tied up her skirts and went up and down the banks of the Onon river, digging wild roots and gathering fruit and onions to feed the children. The boys learned to fish and hunt small game. They grew up hungry and hard.

When Temujin and his brother Qasar killed their half-brother Begter in a quarrel over a fish, Hoelun was furious. She told them they had no friends but their own shadows and no whips but their horses' tails, and that they should be uniting against their enemies, not killing each other. Temujin later united the Mongol tribes. He kept his mother close and valued her counsel.
lesson: A parent's strength in the worst times becomes the child's first lesson in survival. Holding a family together sometimes means feeding it and scolding it with equal force.
source: The Secret History of the Mongols, sections 73 to 78, trans. Igor de Rachewiltz (2004)
caveat: The Secret History mixes history with legend, and its dates are uncertain.
